implementation_notes: Java's creation owner is normally a static factory method on the aggregate: named, able to return a subtype or a cached instance, and compatible with keeping the constructor private (Effective Java Item 1). A dedicated factory class is the fallback when creation needs injected collaborators. The standard library supplies the factory-as-value forms - java.util.function.Supplier and ServiceLoader.Provider - so a creator can be selected or discovered at runtime instead of compiled in, and in Spring applications @Bean methods or FactoryBean make the container the creation owner for wired components. Persistence frameworks reconstitute entities without calling the factory, so keep a separate package-private reconstitution method and never let invariants depend on construction having gone through the public path.
pitfalls: A private constructor does not stop frameworks: JPA/Hibernate and Jackson create instances through reflection, bypassing the factory and its validation.
Using exceptions for expected validation failures turns a domain answer into control flow; return an Optional/Result-style value and reserve exceptions for programmer errors.
Factories that cache or pool products share mutable state; document and synchronize them, or keep the factory stateless.

variants.name: Supplier registry (creators as values)
variants.implementation_notes: When the product type is chosen from runtime data, store creators instead of branches: Map<String, Supplier<Payment>> (or an enum implementing Supplier) is the factory, and ServiceLoader.Provider is the standard discovery mechanism when providers arrive on the classpath; both make the creator a first-class value that can be registered, replaced in tests and listed without reflection.
pitfalls: Supplier.get() cannot report failure; use a checked creator interface (Function<Raw, Payment> or a custom factory type) when creation can fail.
ServiceLoader providers need the module's uses directive, otherwise they are silently invisible; a registry built from a Map.of is fine for closed sets.
Lambdas have no meaningful toString/equals; key the registry by explicit names, never by supplier identity.

variants.name: Spring container-owned factory (@Bean / FactoryBean)
variants.implementation_notes: In a Spring application the container owns creation: an @Bean method inside a @Configuration class declares a factory whose dependencies are injected as method parameters (inter-bean references are proxied), and a FactoryBean is the explicit factory object when the product's type differs from the factory's. Use it for application-level creators - repositories, gateways, factories that need other beans - and keep domain validation inside the domain factory that the bean method delegates to.
pitfalls: Lite-mode configuration (a class not annotated @Configuration) is not proxied; calling one @Bean method from another builds a new instance instead of returning the bean.
A FactoryBean is injected by its product type; ask for the factory itself with the &name prefix, or injection points silently get the product.
Bean methods that validate and wire at once become the god factory in Java clothing; delegate to the domain factory.
